title: Every face
hook: Jews of every color and background
carry: a whole story, not a question

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ger tzedek, the Jew by choice, and the line fully Jewish. Did you welcome someone who chose? Today the welcome widens to the whole room. Day one thousand forty-seven.

"And a mixed multitude went up also with them." That's a line from the book of Exodus, about the night the Israelites walked out of Egypt. Not one family. Not one look. A crowd, and the text goes out of its way to say that others walked out with them. Now step into a synagogue on a Saturday morning. The woman handing out prayer books may trace her family to Baghdad. The man beside you, to Addis Ababa, or Kraków, or Kochi, or a small town where nobody else was Jewish. A child in the front row was adopted. Someone at the back chose this people as an adult. Today is about every face in that room.
screen: `A MIXED MULTITUDE.` → `BAGHDAD, ADDIS ABABA, KRAKÓW, KOCHI.` → `EVERY FACE IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, the early collection of rabbinic teaching, asks a strange question. Why did God begin with just one person, one Adam, instead of a whole crowd? It offers several answers. One is so that nobody could ever say to anyone else, my ancestor was greater than yours. Everyone goes back to the same one. Then it reaches for a picture from the mint. When a king stamps coins from one die, every coin comes out the same. God stamped every human being with the seal of the first person, and not one of them is like another. So in this teaching, sameness is the human way of making things. Difference is the divine signature. The prophet Amos says something sharper still. Speaking for God to his own people, he asks: "Are ye not as the children of the Ethiopians unto Me, O children of Israel?" Readers hear the line in more than one way. Some hear a warning against pride: being chosen doesn't put you closer to God than a far-off nation. Others hear it as an embrace that reaches all the way to Africa. Either way, the verse sets Israel and a distant people side by side in God's eyes. The faces of the Jewish people tell that story out loud. Beta Israel from Ethiopia, with their own prayers and the festival of Sigd. The Jews of Cochin in India. Families from Yemen, Iraq, Morocco and Iran. Ashkenazi families from Europe. Jews by choice, and children of every color growing up in Jewish homes. Some Jews of color have described being asked, again and again, are you really Jewish? Yesterday's lesson already answered: someone who belongs, belongs. So today's line is two words, every face. Each face is a whole story, not a question to be checked at the door.
screen: `WHY GOD BEGAN WITH ONE PERSON.` · `ONE SEAL, AND NO TWO COINS ALIKE.` · `AS THE CHILDREN OF THE ETHIOPIANS.` · `A WHOLE STORY BEHIND EACH FACE.` · then, large: `EVERY FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one new story. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a Jewish community you know little about. Ethiopia. India. Yemen. Iran. Or one Jewish person whose family took a road unlike any you know. Hold the questions softly. Where did their grandparents walk? What did they carry? What did they sing on the way? You don't need the answers now. Just make room for them, the way the Mishnah makes room for a face unlike any other. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people of every look who belong. If you don't, simply hold that one community in mind. The bell holds the time.
Every face. The Mishnah's picture: God stamps every person from one seal, and no two come out alike. Today's word.

Your line: a whole story, not a question. Today, when you meet someone new, try trading the question where are you really from for a warmer one: what's your story? Then listen to the whole answer. Day one thousand forty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish communities and organizations share the histories of Ethiopian, Indian, Mizrahi, Sephardi, Ashkenazi and other Jews through study, festivals, food and personal stories, and some congregations make a point of welcoming Jews of color and Jews by choice.

fork.setup: you're a king with one die for stamping coins. you strike it again and again. what comes out?
options: every coin different from the last.
a few the same, a few different.
fork.reveal: a king's coins all come out the same. the Mishnah's surprise is that God stamps every person from one seal, and not one of them is like another.

original.note: Hebrew: face. In biblical Hebrew the word is plural in form, even for a single face.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jews all come from one place and look one way.
what it means: Jews have roots in Ethiopia, India, Yemen, Iraq, Morocco, Iran, Europe and beyond, and some chose to join.
what a scholar hears: the Mishnah's one Adam, so no one can boast of an ancestor, and Amos setting Israel beside the Ethiopians.
